title: Candy
description: Brute force to optimized: repeatedly rescanning to fix violations versus two fixed single-direction passes combined by max.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: There are n children standing in a line, each with a rating value ratings[i]. Each child must receive at least one candy, and any child with a HIGHER rating than an adjacent neighbor must receive MORE candies than that neighbor. Return the MINIMUM total candies needed.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Each child's candy count depends on BOTH left and right neighbors\"","Two separate passes, one enforcing each direction's constraint, combined via a max"],["A local comparative constraint (higher rating needs more candy than a specific neighbor)","A greedy left-to-right pass handles the left-neighbor constraint; a right-to-left pass handles the right-neighbor constraint"]]}

blocks.text: Each child's minimum candy count is driven by TWO separate constraints (relative to their left neighbor, and relative to their right neighbor), which can each be satisfied independently with a single directional pass, and then combined by taking the maximum requirement from each pass for every child.

blocks.title: Analogy: Awarding Bonus Points Based on Being Better Than Both Neighbors
blocks.text: Picture awarding a minimum bonus to people in a line, where anyone rated higher than the person to their LEFT needs more bonus than them, and independently, anyone rated higher than the person to their RIGHT also needs more bonus than THEM. Handling each direction separately, then taking whichever requirement is stricter for each person, satisfies both simultaneously.

blocks.caption: A left-to-right pass enforces the left-neighbor rule; a right-to-left pass enforces the right-neighbor rule, combined by max

blocks.text: Result: 5. Candy counts [2,1,2]: child 0 (rating 1) gets more than child 1 (rating 0); child 2 (rating 2) gets more than child 1.

Before repeatedly rescanning to fix constraint violations, notice that the left-neighbor constraint and right-neighbor constraint can each be handled with a SINGLE dedicated pass, and combining both results (taking the max needed for each child) simultaneously satisfies both requirements.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A left-to-right pass, giving each child one more candy than their LEFT neighbor whenever their rating is higher, correctly satisfies the "higher rating than left neighbor needs more candy" constraint in isolation.

Observation 2: A separate right-to-left pass, giving each child one more candy than their RIGHT neighbor whenever their rating is higher, correctly satisfies the "higher rating than right neighbor needs more candy" constraint in isolation, taking the MAXIMUM with whatever the left-to-right pass already assigned (since a child might need to satisfy BOTH constraints simultaneously).

Observation 3: Every child starts with a baseline of 1 candy (the minimum guarantee), before either pass potentially increases it.

Observation 4: Combining both passes' results via max ensures every child's final candy count satisfies both their left AND right neighbor constraints simultaneously, and the sum of all these final counts is the true minimum total.

This leads to two passes: left-to-right, incrementing from the left neighbor when rating increases; right-to-left, taking the max with incrementing from the right neighbor when rating increases (relative to the right neighbor). Sum the final array.
Start everyone with 1 candy, then repeatedly scan the array, giving any child violating a neighbor constraint one more candy than that neighbor, looping until no more violations exist.

items: Initialize every child's candy count to 1.
Repeatedly scan the array for any child whose rating is higher than a neighbor but whose candy count is not yet higher than that neighbor's.
Fix any such violation by increasing that child's candy count, and repeat until a full scan finds no violations.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Repeatedly scanning and fixing violations directly implements the constraint-satisfaction definition.
This could require O(n) full passes to fully converge in the worst case (e.g., a long strictly ascending or descending run), costing O(n squared) overall.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) in the worst case, due to repeated full rescans.
Space: O(n) for the candy array.

Limitation: two FIXED, single-direction passes (left-to-right, then right-to-left), each handling one constraint direction completely, replace the repeated rescanning with a guaranteed O(n) total solution.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why repeated rescanning is unnecessary: the left-neighbor constraint can be FULLY satisfied in a single left-to-right pass (each child only ever needs to look at the neighbor already finalized to their left), and the right-neighbor constraint similarly in a single right-to-left pass.

The two-pass combination: after the left-to-right pass assigns each child at least enough candy relative to their left neighbor, the right-to-left pass revisits each child, taking the MAXIMUM of their current count and (right neighbor's count + 1) whenever their rating exceeds the right neighbor's.

Why taking the max is essential: a child might need MORE candy to satisfy the right-neighbor constraint than what the left-to-right pass already gave them (or vice versa), so combining via max ensures BOTH constraints hold simultaneously.

The core idea: two fixed, single-direction passes, combined by max, fully resolve both constraints in guaranteed O(n) total time.

Left-to-right pass: for each child, if rating exceeds the left neighbor's, set candy to left neighbor's candy + 1. Right-to-left pass: for each child, if rating exceeds the right neighbor's, set candy to the MAX of its current value and (right neighbor's candy + 1). Sum the final array.

blocks.caption: Two fixed passes, combined by max, satisfy both left and right neighbor constraints

blocks.text: The left-to-right pass fully and correctly satisfies the left-neighbor constraint alone, since each child only ever depends on their (already finalized) left neighbor. The right-to-left pass then does the same for the right-neighbor constraint, and taking the MAX with the already-assigned value ensures neither pass's requirement is ever violated by the other, since a higher requirement from either direction always wins. This two-pass combination therefore satisfies BOTH constraints for every child simultaneously, achieving the true minimum total.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), two linear passes.
Space: O(n) for the candy array.

blocks.text: Candy is a classic example of decomposing a bidirectional constraint into two independent, single-direction passes, then combining the results via max, a technique reused across many "satisfy constraints from both sides" problems.

items: Using assignment instead of max in the right-to-left pass, potentially undoing progress already made by the left-to-right pass.
Forgetting the baseline of 1 candy per child before either pass runs.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "two separate single-direction passes, combined by max" clarifies why this is NOT simply two independent answers being added, but rather each child's TRUE requirement being the stricter of the two.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "a constraint that depends on BOTH left and right neighbors", think: two separate single-direction passes, combined by taking the maximum.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Repeated rescan-and-fix costs up to O(n squared) time in the worst case; two fixed passes combined by max cost O(n) time, both using O(n) space.

items: Pattern: two single-direction passes (left-to-right, then right-to-left), combined by taking the maximum for each element.
Core Idea: the left-to-right pass satisfies the left-neighbor constraint; the right-to-left pass satisfies the right-neighbor constraint, taking the max with the already-assigned value.
Time: O(n squared) worst case for repeated rescanning, O(n) for the two-pass approach.
Most Important Observation: a bidirectional constraint can be decomposed into two independent single-direction passes, combined via max.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, moderately hard greedy problem prized for this two-pass decomposition technique.
One line memory trick: left-to-right for the left-neighbor rule, right-to-left (taking the max) for the right-neighbor rule.
